Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A 59-year-old man in coastal southern Norway developed tremor, headache, night sweats and persistent hiccups after a fall with a blow to the back of the head. He has type 2 diabetes and previous thymoma surgery. An initial MRI was reported as unremarkable. Routine blood tests were not explanatory; the initial working diagnosis was post-concussion syndrome.
Symptoms progressed over months to gait difficulty, falls, memory difficulty, dysphagia, resting tremor, bradykinesia and hypophonia. Dopamine-transporter imaging showed reduced uptake, prompting a Parkinson disease hypothesis, but levodopa did not improve symptoms. He was readmitted with worsening weakness, wasting, brisk reflexes and possible fasciculations. Neurophysiological studies were normal. EEG showed mild encephalopathy, and CSF had 443 white cells/microlitre against a reference below 5, with protein 3.03 g/L.
There are no pathogen-specific CSF results, established cause, treatment response or formally reinterpreted MRI findings in this packet. A previously unremarkable report should not be rewritten as proof that no abnormality existed.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Reframe the progressive neurological problem, explain what the new CSF/EEG evidence changes and compare important categories of explanation. State urgent specialist assessment priorities and what earlier records or investigations should be revisited. Do not infer that the fall proved causation or that the dopamine scan established idiopathic Parkinson disease. Use only the supplied information at this decision point. Separate observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent measurements, negative findings, treatment responses or probabilities. Do not give a drug dose or a fixed treatment regimen. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "Reframing the Clinical Problem

Observed facts: Progressive neurological decline over months with tremor, bradykinesia, dysphagia, gait failure, weakness, wasting, brisk reflexes, possible fasciculations, and now CSF showing 443 WBC/µL with protein 3.03 g/L plus EEG encephalopathy. Levodopa produced no improvement. Neurophysiology was normal.

What the CSF/EEG changes: This degree of pleocytosis and protein elevation is incompatible with idiopathic Parkinson disease or post-concussion syndrome. The DaT-SPECT finding cannot be taken as establishing a neurodegenerative diagnosis when an active inflammatory or infective process is present in the CSF. The working diagnosis must now shift to an acquired inflammatory, infective, or autoimmune encephalomyelitis until excluded.

Categories to compare: Infective causes (bacterial, viral, fungal, mycobacterial) given night sweats and CSF profile; autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis given prior thymoma; post-traumatic injury, which does not explain this CSF magnitude; neurodegenerative disease, now poorly supported.

Urgent priorities: Infectious disease and neuroimmunology co-assessment. Pathogen-specific CSF studies (culture, PCR panels, fungal and mycobacterial testing). Autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibody panels. Reinterpretation of the original MRI by neuroradiology with current clinical context. Review of thymoma status for residual or recurrent disease.

Proposed actions: Do not attribute causation to the fall. Do not treat as idiopathic PD.
